Improved Bounds for Online Matching with Random Edge Arrivals

Yilong Feng ††thanks: State Key Lab of IOTSC, University of Macau. Email: yc37459@um.edu.mo.    Haolong Li ††thanks: State Key Lab of IOTSC, University of Macau. Email: yc47435@um.edu.mo.    Zonghan Yang ††thanks: Shanghai Jiao Tong University. Email: fstqwq@sjtu.edu.cn. Part of this work was done while the author was visiting the State Key Lab of IOTSC, University of Macau.
Abstract

We study the unweighted online matching problem with random edge arrivals, where each edge arrives at an independent time drawn uniformly from [0,1][0,1], and the algorithm must immediately and irrevocably accept or reject it while maintaining a matching. Guruganesh and Singla (IPCO, 2017) first broke the 1/21/2 barrier of the naive Greedy algorithm by giving a (1/2+ε)(1/2+\varepsilon)-competitive algorithm for a small constant ε>0\varepsilon>0, a guarantee that has remained the best known for nearly a decade. We give a simple three-phase algorithm that achieves a competitive ratio of 0.54450.5445 by deliberately rejecting selected early edges to reserve their endpoints for later matching opportunities. With a different choice of parameters, the same algorithm is 0.55350.5535-competitive on triangle-free graphs, including bipartite graphs. We also establish competitive ratio upper bounds below 0.69640.6964 for general graphs and 0.70430.7043 for bipartite graphs via exact rational evaluation of an optimal-policy recurrence on fixed graphs, even when the input graph is known up to isomorphism.

1 Introduction

Online matching has been a central topic in online algorithms since the seminal work of Karp, Vazirani and Vazirani [22] on online bipartite matching. In this one-sided vertex-arrival model, the optimal competitive ratio is 1−1/e1-1/e under adversarial arrivals [1, 6, 8], while strictly larger ratios are achievable under a uniformly random arrival order [21, 23]. In the more general edge-arrival model, edges of an underlying graph arrive sequentially, and the algorithm must immediately and irrevocably accept or reject each arriving edge while maintaining a matching. Its performance is measured by the competitive ratio, the worst-case ratio of its expected matching size to the maximum matching size.

Under adversarial edge arrivals, the simple Greedy algorithm, which matches every arriving edge whenever possible, is 1/21/2-competitive. Gamlath, Kapralov, Maggiori, Svensson and Wajc [13] proved that no randomized algorithm can do better even on bipartite graphs. A natural question is whether random edge arrivals, where the adversary chooses the graph while the edges arrive in a uniformly random order, permit a substantially better guarantee. Unfortunately, Greedy’s competitive ratio remains 1/21/2, even on bipartite graphs [7, 16]. Guruganesh and Singla [16] first broke the 1/21/2 barrier, achieving 0.500090.50009 on bipartite graphs and 1/2+ε1/2+\varepsilon on general graphs for a small constant ε>0\varepsilon>0, assuming the number of edges mm is known in advance.11 1 Their Marking-Greedy algorithm and analysis extend to independent uniform arrival times in [0,1][0,1] with the same competitive guarantees, using time thresholds for the phases without advance knowledge of mm. We discuss the distinctions between these arrival models in Section 1.3. On the impossibility side, the best known upper bounds are 47/60≈0.783347/60\approx 0.7833 for general graphs [11] and 23/28≈0.821423/28\approx 0.8214 for bipartite graphs [16].

1.1 Our Model and Results

We study online matching with random edge arrivals in continuous time. For an unknown finite simple graph G⁡(V,E)G(V,E) with a maximum matching M∗M^{*} of size 𝖮𝖯𝖳=|M∗|\mathsf{OPT}=|M^{*}|, each edge e∈Ee\in E arrives at an independent time te∼U⁡[0,1]t_{e}\sim U[0,1]. The algorithm observes each arriving edge together with its arrival time, but knows neither GG nor m=|E|m=|E|. Let 𝖠𝖫𝖦\mathsf{ALG} be the size of the matching it produces; its competitive ratio is defined as infG{𝔼⁡[𝖠𝖫𝖦]/𝖮𝖯𝖳}\inf_{G}\{\mathbb{E}[\mathsf{ALG}]/\mathsf{OPT}\}. We improve both the lower and upper bounds on the optimal competitive ratio, as shown in Figure 1.

Lower bounds.

We propose a three-phase algorithm called Reserve-Retain-Recover, which partitions the edge stream by the observed arrival times without prior knowledge of GG or mm. We analyze its competitive ratio in Sections 2, 3 and 4. With a different choice of parameters, the same algorithm achieves a stronger guarantee on triangle-free graphs; see Appendix B.

Theorem 1.1 (General lower bound).

There exists a 0.54450.5445-competitive algorithm for online matching with random edge arrivals.

Theorem 1.2 (Triangle-free lower bound).

There exists a 0.55350.5535-competitive algorithm for online matching with random edge arrivals on triangle-free graphs, including bipartite graphs.

Upper bounds.

In Section 5, we give the input graph to the algorithm up to isomorphism, while choosing its vertex labeling and edge arrival order uniformly at random. The optimal online algorithm under this uncertainty can be described as a dynamic program. Evaluating the recurrence on the hard instances G10G_{10} and B2,3,3B_{2,3,3} (Figure 2) yields the following upper bounds.

Theorem 1.3 (General upper bound).

Even when the input graph is known up to isomorphism, no online algorithm has a competitive ratio greater than 0.69640.6964 on general graphs.

Theorem 1.4 (Bipartite upper bound).

Even when the input graph is known up to isomorphism, no online algorithm has a competitive ratio greater than 0.70430.7043 on bipartite graphs.

1.2 Our Algorithm and Techniques

We now present Reserve-Retain-Recover (Algorithm 1.2) and the ideas behind the proof of Theorem 1.1.

Algorithm 1: Reserve-Retain-Recover (Parameters: 0≤a<b≤10\leq a<b\leq 1 and 0≤p≤10\leq p\leq 1)  Initialize: matching M←∅M\leftarrow\varnothing, shadow matching T←∅T\leftarrow\varnothing, reserved vertices X←∅X\leftarrow\varnothing. • Phase 1 (Reserve, t∈[0,a)t\in[0,a)): For each arriving edge e=(u,v)e=(u,v), if both u,vu,v are unmatched in TT, add ee to TT (calling it a shadow edge) and flip an independent coin: w.p. pp, discard ee and add both u,vu,v to XX; w.p. 1−p1-p, add ee to MM. Otherwise, discard ee. • Phase 2 (Retain, t∈[a,b)t\in[a,b)): For each arriving edge e=(u,v)e=(u,v), if both u,vu,v are unmatched in TT, add ee to both TT and MM (also calling it a shadow edge). Otherwise, discard ee. • Phase 3 (Recover, t∈[b,1]t\in[b,1]): Let YY be the set of vertices left unmatched in TT at time bb. For each arriving edge e=(u,v)e=(u,v), if both u,vu,v are unmatched in MM and not both in XX (i.e., ee is an X​YXY-edge or a Y​YYY-edge), add ee to MM. Otherwise, discard ee.

Algorithm design.

Consider a sunflower consisting of KnK_{n} with one private leaf attached to each core vertex, as shown in Figure 3. The unique maximum matching contains all nn leaf edges, whereas Greedy matches only n/2+Θ⁡(log⁡n)n/2+\Theta(\log n) edges in expectation under random edge arrivals, giving a ratio of 1/2+Θ⁡(log⁡n/n)1/2+\Theta(\log n/n) on this family.

In this graph, the (n2)\binom{n}{2} core edges vastly outnumber the nn leaf edges: within the first Θ⁡(n​log⁡n)\Theta(n\log n) arrivals, Greedy already matches almost all core vertices, mostly via core edges that each block two edges of the unique perfect matching. Rejecting all edges selected by Greedy in this early prefix to reserve their endpoints, and later matching only reserved vertices to remaining unmatched vertices, recovers almost all leaf edges and achieves a ratio of 1−O⁡(1/log⁡n)1-O(1/\log n). On general graphs, this early-saturation phenomenon is captured by the Hastiness Lemma used by Guruganesh and Singla [16], which shows that whenever Greedy performs close to 1/21/2, it accepts most of its edges early. Based on this property, their Marking-Greedy algorithm maintains the shadow greedy matching TT up to time bb, randomly rejecting a pp-fraction of shadow edges to form a reserved set XX, and in [b,1][b,1] seeks additional matches between XX and the set YY of vertices left unmatched in TT.

On graphs where Greedy already performs well, however, rejecting early shadow edges may sacrifice edges of M∗M^{*} without creating compensating recovery opportunities. In fact, the expected rate at which Greedy accepts edges decreases over time, and in hard instances is heavily concentrated near the very beginning of the stream. This allows Reserve-Retain-Recover to subdivide [0,b)[0,b) more finely into a reserve phase [0,a)[0,a) and an intermediate retain phase [a,b)[a,b): we only reject shadow edges in the earliest phase [0,a)[0,a), accept every new shadow edge during [a,b)[a,b), and defer recovery of the reserved vertices XX to the final phase [b,1][b,1]. At time bb, the vertices unmatched in MM partition into XX and YY, and in the recovery phase [b,1][b,1] the algorithm greedily accepts both X​YXY-edges and Y​YYY-edges. Including Y​YYY-edges provides additional matches, though they may also compete with X​YXY-edges for endpoints in YY; our analysis accounts for both together.

Conditional arrival times.

To analyze the recovery phase, we condition on the shadow matching TT at time bb and the arrival times of its edges, which fixes the unmatched vertex set YY. Consider a shadow edge (x1,x2)(x_{1},x_{2}) selected at time s<as<a and an edge ff between {x1,x2}\{x_{1},x_{2}\} and YY. Had ff arrived before ss, both of its endpoints would have been unmatched in TT and TT would have selected ff; after time ss, ff no longer affects TT. Hence the conditioning only reveals that ff arrives after ss, so its arrival time is uniform on (s,1](s,1], independently of the other edges, and ff arrives in the recovery phase [b,1][b,1] w.p.

qs=1−b1−s.q_{s}=\frac{1-b}{1-s}.

Similarly, every Y​YYY-edge arrives after time bb. Once the reservation choices are fixed, the recovery phase is Greedy on the X​YXY- and Y​YYY-edges that arrive in [b,1][b,1]: each X​YXY-edge appears independently w.p. qsq_{s}, every Y​YYY-edge appears w.p. 11, and these edges arrive in a uniform random order.

Coupling two greedy matchings.

Fix a maximum matching M∗M^{*} and a shadow edge e=(x1,x2)e=(x_{1},x_{2}) from the reserve phase. Reserving x1,x2x_{1},x_{2} gives up ee, so we must account for what the recovery phase gains in return: besides x1x_{1} and x2x_{2}, we track their k≤2k\leq 2 partners in YY under M∗M^{*}, since an edge from xix_{i} to its YY-partner can be blocked during recovery only if at least one of its endpoints is already matched. To measure how the coin flip for ee affects these vertices, we fix the reservation choices of all other shadow edges and couple the two recovery runs of Greedy, without x1,x2x_{1},x_{2} (w.p. 1−p1-p, when ee is accepted) and with x1,x2x_{1},x_{2} in XX (w.p. pp, when x1,x2x_{1},x_{2} are reserved), using the same arrival order on shared edges. Let NN and RR count the matched vertices among {x1,x2}\{x_{1},x_{2}\} and among their YY-partners in the run with x1,x2x_{1},x_{2}, and let KK count the matched YY-partners in the run without them. Averaging over the coin flip for ee, recovery matches p​𝔼​[N]p\,\mathbb{E}[N] vertices in {x1,x2}\{x_{1},x_{2}\} and p​𝔼​[R]+(1−p)​𝔼​[K]p\,\mathbb{E}[R]+(1-p)\,\mathbb{E}[K] of their YY-partners in expectation. Weighting these counts by 3/23/2 and 11 and using 1−p≥p/21-p\geq p/2 (for p≤2/3p\leq 2/3) reduces our local recovery bound (Lemma 2.1),

32​p​𝔼​[N]+p​𝔼​[R]+(1−p)​𝔼​[K]≥p2​𝔼​[3​N+2​R+K]≥3​p2​k,\frac{3}{2}p\,\mathbb{E}[N]+p\,\mathbb{E}[R]+(1-p)\,\mathbb{E}[K]\geq\frac{p}{2}\mathbb{E}[3N+2R+K]\geq\frac{3p}{2}k,

to the coupled comparison 𝔼⁡[3​N+2​R+K]≥3​k\mathbb{E}[3N+2R+K]\geq 3k, proven in Section 4 (Lemma 2.2).

The global bound.

Summing the local bounds over the shadow edges from the reserve phase still leaves graph-dependent terms, such as the number of shadow edges selected in each phase and the number of edges in M∗M^{*} whose endpoints are both unmatched in TT at time bb. We split the probability that both endpoints of e∈M∗e\in M^{*} are unmatched in TT at time tt into

Pr⁡[e​ arrives after ​t]⋅Pr⁡[both endpoints of ​e​ are unmatched at ​t​ in ​G∖{e}].\Pr[e\text{ arrives after }t]\cdot\Pr[\text{both endpoints of }e\text{ are unmatched at }t\text{ in }G\setminus\{e\}].

Let re​(t)r_{e}(t) denote the latter probability, which we call the survival probability of ee up to time tt. In Section 2, we express all graph-dependent terms as a global lower bound that is linear in r⁡(t)r(t), the average of re​(t)r_{e}(t) over e∈M∗e\in M^{*}, retaining information at both phase boundaries and throughout the retain phase rather than relying only on a hastiness bound for early edges. A key observation is that re​(t)r_{e}(t) (and hence r⁡(t)r(t)) is a convex combination of the powers (1−t)n(1-t)^{n} for integers n≥0n\geq 0. Intuitively, (1−t)n(1-t)^{n} is the probability that none of nn independent edges have arrived by time tt, which contributes to the event that both endpoints of ee are unmatched at time tt. We formalize this observation in Lemma 3.1. By linearity, it suffices to evaluate the global bound on each power separately. We then choose a,b,pa,b,p and verify the resulting scalar inequalities to obtain the competitive ratio of 0.54450.5445.

1.3 Related Work

Due to the vast literature on online matching, here we only review the most relevant ones. For broader accounts, we refer to the excellent surveys of Mehta [25] and Huang, Tang and Wajc [17].

Online bipartite matching with random vertex arrivals.

Goel and Mehta [14] showed that Greedy is (1−1/e)(1-1/e)-competitive in this model. Karande, Mehta and Tripathi [21] and Mahdian and Yan [23] analyzed Ranking, obtaining ratios of 0.6530.653 and 0.6960.696, respectively. Huang, Tang, Wu and Zhang [18] extended Ranking to the vertex-weighted case, where offline vertices have nonnegative weights, and achieved a competitive ratio of 0.65340.6534. The ratio was later improved to 0.66290.6629 by Jin and Williamson [20], 0.68620.6862 by Peng and Tang [26], and 0.69800.6980 by Peng and Tang [27].

Variants of online matching with edge arrivals.

Competitive ratios better than 0.50.5 are known under structural or distributional relaxations for online matching with edge arrivals. Buchbinder, Segev and Tkach [2] gave a 5/95/9-competitive algorithm on trees with adversarial edge arrivals; with free disposal, Jiang and Zhang [19] achieved 5/85/8 on forests and 2/32/3 on growing trees, where each arriving edge introduces a new leaf. Dyer and Frieze [7] gave a nearly tight ratio of 0.76900.7690 for Greedy on trees under random edge arrivals. Gravin, Tang and Wang [15] assumed that edges of a given bipartite graph arrive in an order chosen by an oblivious adversary and are independently realized with known probabilities, and gave a 0.5030.503-competitive algorithm. When edges are sampled independently and identically from a known distribution, Feng, Li and Wu [12] beat 1−1/e1-1/e under integral arrival rates. For edge-weighted online matching with random edge arrivals, Ezra, Feldman, Gravin and Tang [10] gave a 1/41/4-competitive algorithm.

Arrival times and advance information.

Assuming that elements arrive at independent uniform times in [0,1][0,1] is a common convention for random order models in the online algorithms literature, e.g., in online bipartite matching with random vertex arrivals [18, 20, 26, 27], prophet secretary [3, 5, 9], and sample-driven optimal stopping [4]. For random edge arrivals, the algorithms of Guruganesh and Singla [16] assume that mm is known in advance; when mm is unknown and the algorithm observes only the arrival order, they proved an upper bound of 2/32/3 by hiding which of several graphs of different sizes is presented. Together with our observed-time model and the setting where the algorithm knows the input graph up to isomorphism, these information settings satisfy

unknown ​m⪯observed times⪯known ​m⪯known graph,\text{unknown }m\ \preceq\ \text{observed times}\ \preceq\ \text{known }m\ \preceq\ \text{known graph},

where A⪯BA\preceq B means that every randomized strategy in AA can be simulated in BB with the same expected matching size on each graph. For example:

  • •

    To simulate observed times in the known-mm permutation model, sample mm independent uniform timestamps in [0,1][0,1], and assign the ii-th smallest timestamp to the ii-th arriving edge; this reproduces the desired joint distribution of edge order and arrival times.

  • •

    Conversely, when mm is also given in the arrival-time model, using the edge order alone recovers the known-mm permutation model.

Thus, when mm is known, the arrival-time and random-permutation models are equivalent. Hence our lower bound also holds in the known-mm permutation model, and our upper bounds hold in all four settings.

2.1 A Local Recovery Bound

Consider a shadow edge e=(x1,x2)∈Tae=(x_{1},x_{2})\in T_{a}. An edge of M∗M^{*} may connect an endpoint of ee to a vertex v∈Yv\in Y. We call such a vertex vv a reference vertex of ee. In particular, if ee is not reserved, then N^e=0\hat{N}_{e}=0, but its reference vertices may still get matched during Phase 3.

The following lemma lower-bounds (the weighted sum of) the expected contribution from N^e\hat{N}_{e} and R^e\hat{R}_{e} in terms of kek_{e}.

Conditional on HbH_{b}, for any p∈[0,2/3]p\in[0,2/3] and every shadow edge e∈Tae\in T_{a}, we have

3 Polynomial Expansion and the Competitive Ratio

The lower bound we derived in Inequality (6) depends on GG through r⁡(t)r(t). In this section, we first show that r⁡(t)r(t) admits a polynomial expansion in powers of 1−t1-t, with nonnegative coefficients summing to 11. This allows us to evaluate the bound one power at a time. We then choose aa and bb, and prove that the resulting bound is at least 0.54450.5445.

3.1 Survival Probabilities as Convex Combinations of Powers

We first consider the probability that an arbitrary set of vertices remains unmatched. The following lemma will apply to each function re​(t)r_{e}(t) defined in Section 2.4.

Lemma 3.1.

Consider running Greedy on a graph JJ where edges have independent and uniform arrival times in [0,1][0,1]. For any vertex set A⊆V⁡(J)A\subseteq V(J) and any time t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1], let P⁡(J,A,t)P(J,A,t) be the probability that all vertices in AA are unmatched at tt. Then there exist coefficients cn≥0c_{n}\geq 0, only finitely many of which are nonzero, so that

P⁡(J,A,t)=∑n≥1cn⋅(1−t)n−1,∑n≥1cn=1.P(J,A,t)=\sum_{n\geq 1}c_{n}\cdot(1-t)^{n-1},\qquad\sum_{n\geq 1}c_{n}=1.
Proof.

We prove the statement by induction on |E⁡(J)||E(J)|, for all choices of AA. If E⁡(J)=∅E(J)=\varnothing, then P⁡(J,A,t)=1P(J,A,t)=1. The statement holds trivially with c1=1c_{1}=1.

Suppose that E⁡(J)≠∅E(J)\neq\varnothing. If all vertices in AA are unmatched at time tt, then either they remain unmatched until the end of the run (which happens w.p. P⁡(J,A,1)P(J,A,1)), or there is an edge with an endpoint in AA that arrives at some time s∈(t,1]s\in(t,1] and is matched by Greedy.

For the second event, fix an edge ee with V⁡(e)∩A≠∅V(e)\cap A\neq\varnothing and condition on its arrival time te=st_{e}=s. Before time ss, Greedy makes the same decisions on JJ and J−eJ-e. Thus, ee is the first edge with an endpoint in AA matched by Greedy if and only if all vertices in A∪V⁡(e)A\cup V(e) are unmatched right before ss in Greedy on J−eJ-e. Integrating over the uniform arrival time of ee and summing over the possible choices of ee, we obtain

P(J,A,t)=P(J,A,1)+∑e∈E⁡(J):V⁡(e)∩A≠∅∫t1P(J−e,A∪V(e),s)ds.P(J,A,t)=P(J,A,1)+\sum_{e\in E(J):V(e)\cap A\neq\varnothing}\int_{t}^{1}P(J-e,A\cup V(e),s)\,ds. (7)

Each graph J−eJ-e has fewer edges than JJ. By the induction hypothesis, each integrand of the RHS is a finite nonnegative combination of powers (1−s)n−1(1-s)^{n-1}. Moreover,

∫t1c⋅(1−s)n−1​𝑑s=cn⋅(1−t)n.\int_{t}^{1}c\cdot(1-s)^{n-1}\,ds=\frac{c}{n}\cdot(1-t)^{n}.

Therefore, Equation (7) expresses P⁡(J,A,t)P(J,A,t) as a finite nonnegative combination of powers of 1−t1-t, including the constant term P⁡(J,A,1)P(J,A,1). Finally, at time t=0t=0, we have

∑n≥1cn=P⁡(J,A,0)=1,\sum_{n\geq 1}c_{n}=P(J,A,0)=1,

which completes the induction. ∎

For each e=(u,v)∈M∗e=(u,v)\in M^{*}, applying Lemma 3.1 with J=G−eJ=G-e and A={u,v}A=\{u,v\} gives the stated representation for re​(t)r_{e}(t). Averaging over e∈M∗e\in M^{*} preserves both nonnegativity and the sum of the coefficients. Hence, there exist coefficients cn≥0c_{n}\geq 0, only finitely many of which are nonzero, so that

r⁡(t)=∑n≥1cn⋅(1−t)n−1,∑n≥1cn=1.r(t)=\sum_{n\geq 1}c_{n}\cdot(1-t)^{n-1},\qquad\sum_{n\geq 1}c_{n}=1. (8)

4 Local Greedy Comparison

We first describe the remaining randomness after conditioning on HbH_{b} and BB in Section 4.1. We then prove Lemma 2.2 for the cases when ke=1k_{e}=1 and ke=2k_{e}=2 in Sections 4.2 and 4.3, respectively.

4.1 Conditional Arrival Times

Recall that HbH_{b} records TbT_{b} and the arrival times of its edges. Conditional on HbH_{b}, we also fix an edge e=(x1,x2)∈Tae=(x_{1},x_{2})\in T_{a}, and define BB to be the graph on (X∪Y)∖{x1,x2}(X\cup Y)\setminus\{x_{1},x_{2}\} containing all Y​YYY-edges and all X​YXY-edges arriving after time bb. Let τv\tau_{v} be the arrival time of the shadow edge matching vv for each v∈V⁡(Tb)v\in V(T_{b}); let τv=+∞\tau_{v}=+\infty for each v∈Yv\in Y.

Lemma 4.1.

Conditional on HbH_{b}, the arrival times of all edges outside TbT_{b} are mutually independent. For each edge (u,v)∈E∖Tb(u,v)\in E\setminus T_{b}, we have

t(u,v)∼U⁡(min⁡{τu,τv,b},1).t_{(u,v)}\sim U\left(\min\{\tau_{u},\tau_{v},b\},1\right).
Proof.

For fixed HbH_{b}, the arrival times of all remaining edges (u,v)∈E∖Tb(u,v)\in E\setminus T_{b} must satisfy t(u,v)>min⁡{τu,τv,b}t_{(u,v)}>\min\{\tau_{u},\tau_{v},b\}. These constraints also suffice to reproduce the same shadow matching and its arrival times. Indeed, when processing edges in arrival order, every edge outside TbT_{b} that arrives before bb has an endpoint already matched by an earlier shadow edge, so it is rejected; the recorded shadow edges are therefore accepted as before. Thus, conditioning on HbH_{b} imposes only these separate constraints on the remaining edges. Their arrival times remain independent, and each is uniformly distributed on its allowed interval. ∎

Let the fixed edge e=(x1,x2)e=(x_{1},x_{2}) arrive at time s<as<a. We further condition on BB. Since the edges between {x1,x2}\{x_{1},x_{2}\} and YY are not used to determine BB, Lemma 4.1 indicates that their arrival times remain mutually independent, each distributed as U⁡(s,1)U(s,1). Hence, each such edge arrives after bb (or in other words, appears in BeB_{e}), independently w.p.

q=1−b1−s≥1−b≥58.q=\frac{1-b}{1-s}\geq 1-b\geq\frac{5}{8}.

Conditional on which of these edges arrive after bb, all edges of BeB_{e} have independent arrival times distributed as U⁡(b,1)U(b,1). We can thus generate the coupled matchings M⁡(B)M(B) and M⁡(Be)M(B_{e}) as follows.

Equivalent formulation of the coupled matchings.

Choose a uniform random order σ\sigma of all edges of BB and all edges between {x1,x2}\{x_{1},x_{2}\} and YY. Independently, retain each edge between {x1,x2}\{x_{1},x_{2}\} and YY w.p. qq. To obtain M⁡(Be)M(B_{e}), run Greedy in the chosen order σ\sigma, skipping the edges between {x1,x2}\{x_{1},x_{2}\} and YY that are not retained. To obtain M⁡(B)M(B), use the same order σ\sigma but skip all edges between {x1,x2}\{x_{1},x_{2}\} and YY.

For the rest of this section, we keep HbH_{b} and BB fixed and consider this equivalent formulation. We write k=kek=k_{e} and omit the conditioning on HbH_{b} and BB from the notation. Our goal is to prove

𝔼⁡[3​N+2​R+K]≥3​k.\mathbb{E}[3N+2R+K]\geq 3k. (10)

Since N,R,KN,R,K are nonnegative, the inequality is immediate when k=0k=0. It remains to consider the cases when k=1k=1 and k=2k=2.

4.2 One Reference Vertex

We first consider the graph with only one of x1,x2x_{1},x_{2}, say x1x_{1}, added to BB. Let C=Be−x2C=B_{e}-x_{2}, and let M⁡(C)M(C) be its greedy matching under the edge order σ\sigma. The following lemma allows us to add x2x_{2} back while using the same bound on CC. We defer its proof to Appendix A.

Lemma 4.2.

For every fixed edge order σ\sigma and every choice of retained edges between {x1,x2}\{x_{1},x_{2}\} and YY, we have

3​N+2​R≥3​N1+2​R1.3N+2R\geq 3N_{1}+2R_{1}.

Fix the edge order σ\sigma and which edges incident to x1x_{1}, other than (x1,y1)(x_{1},y_{1}), are retained. The edge (x1,y1)(x_{1},y_{1}) is retained w.p. qq. Let C0C_{0} be the graph obtained by omitting (x1,y1)(x_{1},y_{1}) from CC. Under this conditioning, M⁡(B)M(B) and M⁡(C0)M(C_{0}) are fixed. We distinguish three cases and consider the contribution to 3​N1+2​R1+K3N_{1}+2R_{1}+K.

  • •

    K=1K=1. If N1=1N_{1}=1, the contribution is at least 33. If N1=0N_{1}=0, then no edge incident to x1x_{1} is matched in CC, and Greedy makes the same decisions within BB as M⁡(B)M(B). We have R1=1R_{1}=1, and 3​N1+2​R1+K=33N_{1}+2R_{1}+K=3.

  • •

    K=0K=0 and M⁡(C0)M(C_{0}) matches x1x_{1}. Then M⁡(C)M(C) matches x1x_{1} regardless of whether (x1,y1)(x_{1},y_{1}) is retained or not. Either (x1,y1)(x_{1},y_{1}) is matched in M⁡(C)M(C), or Greedy makes the same decisions as on C0C_{0}. Thus N1=1N_{1}=1, and the contribution is at least 33.

  • •

    K=0K=0 and M⁡(C0)M(C_{0}) does not match x1x_{1}. Since no edge incident to x1x_{1} is accepted in C0C_{0}, its greedy matching within BB is M⁡(B)M(B). As K=0K=0, both x1x_{1} and y1y_{1} are unmatched in M⁡(C0)M(C_{0}). If (x1,y1)(x_{1},y_{1}) is retained, it gets matched in M⁡(C)M(C), giving N1=R1=1N_{1}=R_{1}=1. If it is not retained, then N1=R1=0N_{1}=R_{1}=0. The conditional expected contribution is (2+3)⋅q=5​q≥25/8>3(2+3)\cdot q=5q\geq 25/8>3.

In every case, the conditional expected contribution is at least 33. Taking expectations over σ\sigma and the retained edges other than (x1,y1)(x_{1},y_{1}) proves Inequality (11). By Lemma 4.2, we have

𝔼⁡[3​N+2​R+K]≥𝔼⁡[3​N1+2​R1+K]≥3,\mathbb{E}[3N+2R+K]\geq\mathbb{E}[3N_{1}+2R_{1}+K]\geq 3,

which proves Lemma 2.2 when k=1k=1.

4.3 Two Reference Vertices

Let the reference vertices of ee be y1y_{1} and y2y_{2} so that (x1,y1),(x2,y2)∈M∗(x_{1},y_{1}),(x_{2},y_{2})\in M^{*}. Applying Lemma 2.2 for k=1k=1 separately to y1y_{1} and y2y_{2} would count 3​N3N twice. We instead condition on the first edge in σ\sigma. For each possible first edge, we separate the contribution of the vertices it matches from the contribution still to be analyzed. For i∈{1,2}i\in\{1,2\}, let μi\mu_{i} be the probability that yiy_{i} is matched in M⁡(B)M(B). Thus, 𝔼⁡[K]=μ1+μ2\mathbb{E}[K]=\mu_{1}+\mu_{2}.

Fix the retention choices of all edges between {x1,x2}\{x_{1},x_{2}\} and Y∖{y1,y2}Y\setminus\{y_{1},y_{2}\}. Let LL count all edges of BB, all retained edges from {x1,x2}\{x_{1},x_{2}\} to Y∖{y1,y2}Y\setminus\{y_{1},y_{2}\}, and all edges from {x1,x2}\{x_{1},x_{2}\} to {y1,y2}\{y_{1},y_{2}\}, regardless of whether retained or not. We prove Lemma 2.2 when k=2k=2 by induction on L≥2L\geq 2. When L=2L=2, the only edges are (x1,y1)(x_{1},y_{1}) and (x2,y2)(x_{2},y_{2}). Each contributes 55 to the LHS of Inequality (10) whenever it is retained. We have

𝔼⁡[3​N+2​R+K]=10​q≥6.\mathbb{E}[3N+2R+K]=10q\geq 6.

Suppose that L>2L>2. Assume that Lemma 2.2 holds for k=2k=2 whenever fewer than LL edges are counted, and both (x1,y1),(x2,y2)(x_{1},y_{1}),(x_{2},y_{2}) exist before retention. Consider the first of these LL edges in σ\sigma. Every edge is equally likely to be first. Conditional on the first edge, the order of the remaining edges is still uniform. We first handle the following two cases.

The first edge ff belongs to BB.

Both M⁡(Be)M(B_{e}) and M⁡(B)M(B) accept ff. Each reference vertex covered by ff contributes 2+1=32+1=3 through 2​R+K2R+K. If neither reference vertex is covered by ff, the induction hypothesis gives an expected contribution of at least 66. If only one reference vertex is covered by ff, Section 4.2 gives an expected contribution of at least 33 from x1,x2x_{1},x_{2} and the reference vertex not covered by ff. If both reference vertices are covered by ff, the contribution is already 66. Thus, for every ff belonging to BB, we have

𝔼⁡[3​N+2​R+K∣f​ is the first]≥6.\mathbb{E}[3N+2R+K\mid f\text{ is the first}]\geq 6.

The first edge joins an endpoint of ee to a non-reference vertex.

By symmetry, let this first edge be (x1,z)(x_{1},z), where z∈Y∖{y1,y2}z\in Y\setminus\{y_{1},y_{2}\}. It is among the LL edges and is retained. Hence, M⁡(Be)M(B_{e}) accepts it, and x1x_{1} contributes 33. After matching (x1,z)(x_{1},z), Greedy continues on Be−{x1,z}B_{e}-\{x_{1},z\}, which consists of B−zB-z together with x2x_{2} and its retained edges to vertices other than zz. We therefore need the following lemma, whose proof is given in Appendix A.

Lemma 4.3.

For i∈{1,2}i\in\{1,2\} and z∈V⁡(B)∖{yi}z\in V(B)\setminus\{y_{i}\}, let DD be the graph obtained from B−zB-z by adding xix_{i} and its retained edges to Y∖{z}Y\setminus\{z\}. Suppose that (xi,yi)(x_{i},y_{i}) is one of the edges retained independently w.p. qq. Let nn and rr indicate whether xix_{i} and yiy_{i} are matched by the greedy matching on DD, respectively. Then

𝔼⁡[3​n+2​r]≥3−μi.\mathbb{E}[3n+2r]\geq 3-\mu_{i}.

By Lemma 4.3, the expected contribution from x2,y2x_{2},y_{2} is at least 3−μ23-\mu_{2}. Together with 𝔼⁡[K]=μ1+μ2\mathbb{E}[K]=\mu_{1}+\mu_{2}, we obtain

𝔼⁡[3​N+2​R+K∣(x1,z)​ is the first]≥3+(3−μ2)+μ1+μ2=6+μ1≥6.\mathbb{E}[3N+2R+K\mid(x_{1},z)\text{ is the first}]\geq 3+(3-\mu_{2})+\mu_{1}+\mu_{2}=6+\mu_{1}\geq 6.

It remains to consider the case when an edge to a reference vertex is the first. Besides (x1,y1)(x_{1},y_{1}) and (x2,y2)(x_{2},y_{2}), there may be neither, one, or both of (x1,y2)(x_{1},y_{2}) and (x2,y1)(x_{2},y_{1}). We call (x1,y2)(x_{1},y_{2}) and (x2,y1)(x_{2},y_{1}) cross edges.

No cross edges.

Assume w.l.o.g. that (x1,y1)(x_{1},y_{1}) is the first. If it is retained, M⁡(Be)M(B_{e}) accepts it: x1x_{1} and y1y_{1} contribute 3+2=53+2=5. After accepting (x1,y1)(x_{1},y_{1}), Greedy continues on the graph consisting of B−y1B-y_{1} together with x2x_{2} and its retained edges. By Lemma 4.3, we have

𝔼⁡[3​N+2​R+K∣(x1,y1)​ is the first and retained]≥5+(3−μ2)+μ1+μ2=8+μ1.\mathbb{E}[3N+2R+K\mid(x_{1},y_{1})\text{ is the first and retained}]\geq 5+(3-\mu_{2})+\mu_{1}+\mu_{2}=8+\mu_{1}.

If it is not retained, the following lemma gives a lower bound of 3+μ13+\mu_{1}.

Lemma 4.4.

If there exists an edge from {x1,x2}\{x_{1},x_{2}\} to yiy_{i} before retention, then

𝔼⁡[3​N+2​R+K]≥3+μ3−i.\mathbb{E}[3N+2R+K]\geq 3+\mu_{3-i}. (12)
Proof.

Apply Inequality (11) with only yiy_{i} counted as a reference vertex, and then use Lemma 4.2 to include the other endpoint of ee. Vertices x1,x2x_{1},x_{2} and yiy_{i} contribute at least 33 to the LHS of Inequality (12), while y3−iy_{3-i} contributes at least μ3−i\mu_{3-i}. ∎

Taking the expectation yields

𝔼⁡[3​N+2​R+K∣(x1,y1)​ is the first]≥q⋅(8+μ1)+(1−q)⋅(3+μ1)=3+5​q+μ1≥6.\mathbb{E}[3N+2R+K\mid(x_{1},y_{1})\text{ is the first}]\geq q\cdot(8+\mu_{1})+(1-q)\cdot(3+\mu_{1})=3+5q+\mu_{1}\geq 6.

One cross edge.

Assume w.l.o.g. that (x1,y2)(x_{1},y_{2}) exists and (x2,y1)(x_{2},y_{1}) does not. We list the conditional lower bounds on 𝔼⁡[3​N+2​R+K]\mathbb{E}[3N+2R+K] for the three possible first edges.

First edge Retained Not retained
(x1,y1)(x_{1},y_{1}) 8+μ18+\mu_{1} 4+μ1−μ24+\mu_{1}-\mu_{2} [Lemma 4.5]
(x2,y2)(x_{2},y_{2}) 8+μ28+\mu_{2} 3+μ23+\mu_{2} [Lemma 4.4]
(x1,y2)(x_{1},y_{2}) 5+μ1+μ25+\mu_{1}+\mu_{2} 66 [Induction hypothesis]

If (x1,y1)(x_{1},y_{1}) or (x2,y2)(x_{2},y_{2}) is the first and retained, the analysis from the previous case applies. If (x1,y2)(x_{1},y_{2}) is first and retained, accepting it contributes 55; adding 𝔼⁡[K]=μ1+μ2\mathbb{E}[K]=\mu_{1}+\mu_{2} gives the stated lower bound.

When (x1,y1)(x_{1},y_{1}) is the first and not retained, we need an additional lower bound. For this case, among the remaining L−1L-1 edges, neither x1x_{1} nor x2x_{2} has an edge connecting to y1y_{1}.

Lemma 4.5.

Assume that the only edges between {x1,x2}\{x_{1},x_{2}\} and {y1,y2}\{y_{1},y_{2}\} before retention are (x1,y2)(x_{1},y_{2}) and (x2,y2)(x_{2},y_{2}). Then we have

𝔼⁡[3​N+2​R+K]≥4+μ1−μ2.\mathbb{E}[3N+2R+K]\geq 4+\mu_{1}-\mu_{2}.

We defer the proof to Appendix A.

If (x2,y2)(x_{2},y_{2}) is not retained, then Lemma 4.4 applies. If (x1,y2)(x_{1},y_{2}) is not retained, the remaining L−1L-1 edges still contain (x1,y1),(x2,y2)(x_{1},y_{1}),(x_{2},y_{2}), so the induction hypothesis applies.

Each of the other L−3L-3 possible first edges has conditional expected contribution at least 66, as shown before. Consequently,

𝔼⁡[3​N+2​R+K]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[3N+2R+K] ≥1L​(6⋅(L−3)+q⋅(21+2​μ1+2​μ2)+(1−q)⋅(13+μ1))\displaystyle\geq\frac{1}{L}\left(6\cdot(L-3)+q\cdot(21+2\mu_{1}+2\mu_{2})+(1-q)\cdot(13+\mu_{1})\right)
≥6⋅(L−3)+13+8​qL≥6,\displaystyle\geq\frac{6\cdot(L-3)+13+8q}{L}\geq 6,

where the last inequality uses q≥5/8q\geq 5/8.

Two cross edges.

All four edges between {x1,x2}\{x_{1},x_{2}\} and {y1,y2}\{y_{1},y_{2}\} exist. Assume w.l.o.g. that (x1,y1)(x_{1},y_{1}) is the first. If it is retained, the same calculation as in the case with no cross edges gives a lower bound of 8+μ1≥68+\mu_{1}\geq 6. If it is not retained, the remaining L−1L-1 edges contain (x1,y2),(x2,y1)(x_{1},y_{2}),(x_{2},y_{1}). Interchange the labels y1y_{1} and y2y_{2}. The induction hypothesis then gives a lower bound of 66.

We have finished the induction. Taking the expectation over the retained edges between {x1,x2}\{x_{1},x_{2}\} and Y∖{y1,y2}Y\setminus\{y_{1},y_{2}\} proves Lemma 2.2 when k=2k=2.

5 Upper Bounds on Graphs Known up to Isomorphism

The thick-𝒵\mathcal{Z} construction of Guruganesh and Singla [16] and the triangle with three leaves of Favrholdt and Vatshelle [11] use the same approach: choose a fixed graph and bound what the algorithm can gain from each possible decision. The four-vertex graph below illustrates this argument.

We formalize this reasoning as an online decision problem on a fixed graph GG with nn vertices, mm edges, and maximum matching size 𝖮𝖯𝖳⁡(G)>0\mathsf{OPT}(G)>0. The algorithm is given GG up to isomorphism, a uniformly random bijection π:V⁡(G)→[n]={0,…,n−1}\pi\colon V(G)\to[n]=\{0,\dots,n-1\} assigns vertex labels, and the edges of π⁡(G)\pi(G) arrive in an independent uniformly random order. Write V⋆​(G)V^{\star}(G) for the maximum expected matching size achievable by an online algorithm in this problem. Averaging over π\pi shows that every online algorithm has some fixed labeling of GG on which its expected matching size is at most V⋆​(G)V^{\star}(G), so no online algorithm achieves a competitive ratio greater than V⋆​(G)/𝖮𝖯𝖳​(G)V^{\star}(G)/\mathsf{OPT}(G).

5.1 Dynamic Program and Optimal Policy

At any step, let HH be the subgraph of edges observed so far and U⊆[n]U\subseteq[n] be the set of currently unmatched labels. Let

C(H)=|{π:V(G)→[n] bijective:E(H)⊆π(E(G))}|C(H)=\bigl|\{\pi\colon V(G)\to[n]\text{ bijective}:E(H)\subseteq\pi(E(G))\}\bigr|

be the number of labelings compatible with HH. When k=|E⁡(H)|<mk=|E(H)|<m, the next arriving edge e∉E⁡(H)e\notin E(H) has distribution

p⁡(e∣H)=C⁡(H+e)(m−k)​C​(H).p(e\mid H)=\frac{C(H+e)}{(m-k)C(H)}. (13)

Define V⁡(H,U)V(H,U) backwards from V⁡(H,U)=0V(H,U)=0 for |E⁡(H)|=m|E(H)|=m by

V⁡(H,U)=∑e∉E⁡(H)C⁡(H+e)>0p⁡(e∣H)​{max⁡{V⁡(H+e,U), 1+V⁡(H+e,U∖e)},e⊆U,V⁡(H+e,U),e⊈U,V(H,U)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}e\notin E(H)\\ C(H+e)>0\end{subarray}}p(e\mid H)\begin{cases}\max\{V(H+e,U),\;1+V(H+e,U\setminus e)\},&e\subseteq U,\\ V(H+e,U),&e\not\subseteq U,\end{cases} (14)

where U∖eU\setminus e removes both endpoints of ee.

Lemma 5.1.

For every graph GG, V⋆​(G)=V⁡(∅,[n])V^{\star}(G)=V(\varnothing,[n]), attained by accepting each feasible arriving edge e⊆Ue\subseteq U if and only if 1+V⁡(H+e,U∖e)≥V⁡(H+e,U)1+V(H+e,U\setminus e)\geq V(H+e,U).

Proof.

Any ordered prefix of kk edges has probability 1/(m(m−1)⋯(m−k+1))1/(m(m-1)\cdots(m-k+1)) under every compatible labeling and zero under all others. Independent of past algorithm choices and of the arrival order within E⁡(H)E(H), the posterior over π\pi is therefore uniform on the C⁡(H)C(H) compatible labelings. Each of the C⁡(H+e)C(H+e) compatible labelings containing ee presents ee next w.p. 1/(m−k)1/(m-k), giving Equation (13). Since HH determines the distribution of future arrivals and UU determines feasibility, (H,U)(H,U) is a sufficient state, and backward induction on m−|E⁡(H)|m-|E(H)| yields Equation (14). ∎

5.2 Upper Bound for General Graphs

Evaluating Equation (14) on the graphs in Figure 5 gives the ratios displayed beneath their names.

Proof of Theorem 1.3.

The 1010-vertex, 1919-edge graph G10G_{10} in Figure 5 has 𝖮𝖯𝖳⁡(G10)=5\mathsf{OPT}(G_{10})=5. Exact rational evaluation of Equation (14) gives

V⋆​(G10)𝖮𝖯𝖳⁡(G10)=29411369116782894223788208640000<0.6964.∎\frac{V^{\star}(G_{10})}{\mathsf{OPT}(G_{10})}=\frac{2941136911678289}{4223788208640000}<0.6964.\qed

5.3 Upper Bound for Bipartite Graphs

Unlike the worst-case general graphs, where G6G_{6} and G10G_{10} omit a single edge to break symmetry and follow no obvious parametric family, exhaustive search over all nonisomorphic bipartite graphs on n=4,6,8,10,12n=4,6,8,10,12 vertices reveals a regular pattern (Figure 6, left). Define Ba1,…,arB_{a_{1},\ldots,a_{r}} by grouping disjoint matching edges into ordered blocks of sizes a1,…,ara_{1},\ldots,a_{r}, then adding every edge from a left endpoint in an earlier block to a right endpoint in a later block. The original edges form the unique perfect matching, as matching the blocks in order shows. Searching larger members of this family yields the sixteen-vertex graph B2,3,3B_{2,3,3} (Figure 6, right).

Proof of Theorem 1.4.

The graph B2,3,3B_{2,3,3} in Figure 6 has 1616 vertices, 2929 edges, and 𝖮𝖯𝖳⁡(B2,3,3)=8\mathsf{OPT}(B_{2,3,3})=8. Exact rational evaluation of Equation (14) gives

V⋆​(B2,3,3)𝖮𝖯𝖳⁡(B2,3,3)=39709690416948790551112075638303485447723417600000<0.7043.∎\frac{V^{\star}(B_{2,3,3})}{\mathsf{OPT}(B_{2,3,3})}=\frac{3970969041694879055111207}{5638303485447723417600000}<0.7043.\qed

Extension to larger nn.

One might ask whether simply scaling up the block sizes, such as considering Bk,k,kB_{k,k,k} for large kk, yields a strong asymptotic upper bound. Unfortunately, this is not the case: like the sunflower graph in Figure 3, Bk,k,kB_{k,k,k} has Θ⁡(n2)\Theta(n^{2}) cross-block edges and only n/2n/2 matching edges, so an online algorithm can achieve a competitive ratio of 1−O⁡(1/log⁡n)1-O(1/\log n) by rejecting early edges. Scaling to larger nn therefore requires a more careful construction.

5.4 Implementation and Verification

We evaluate Equation (14) with three implementations33 3 Our code is available at https://github.com/fstqwq/Random-Order-Matching-Upper-Bounds., each serving a different purpose; Table 1 compares their running times.

Python reference.

A concise Python program evaluates Equation (14) in exact rational arithmetic, memoizing states (H,U)(H,U) and using nauty [24] to identify states up to consistent vertex relabeling. Although its worst-case running time is O⁡(2m+n​n!​poly​(n))O(2^{m+n}\,n!\,\mathrm{poly}(n)), far fewer states are reached in practice: on G10G_{10}, the Python program visits 10 44710\,447 isomorphism classes of observed subgraphs and finishes in about two minutes.

Lean verification.

To certify this computation, we wrote a second solver in Lean 4 and proved a theorem about its output. Fix a nonempty graph GG, and average over all n!n! labelings π\pi and all m!m! arrival orders of π⁡(G)\pi(G). The theorem states that for every online strategy, deterministic or randomized with rational probabilities, the expected number of accepted edges divided by 𝖮𝖯𝖳⁡(G)\mathsf{OPT}(G) is at most the value returned by the solver. The proof first establishes this bound for the unreduced recurrence (14), and then shows that relabeling states by any vertex permutation, as the solver does, leaves the value unchanged. The Lean solver is much slower than the Python program; on G10G_{10}, it reproduces the exact value in Theorem 1.3.

C++ solver.

For larger graphs, a multithreaded C++ solver evaluates Equation (14) in exact arithmetic by parallel memoized search using a shared memoization table. In Lean 4, we prove the correctness of the underlying recurrence and memoization invariants: whenever each subproblem call or cache hit returns its true value, each step computes the exact value regardless of the vertex relabeling or summation order. The C++ solver implements this verified recurrence directly44 4 Under standard runtime and external library assumptions documented in the repository, e.g., the correctness of the concurrent hash map.; all three solvers also return identical exact ratios on G4,G6,G8,G10G_{4},G_{6},G_{8},G_{10} and every nonisomorphic graph on at most seven vertices.

Exhaustive search.

To find worst-case general instances on n≤11n\leq 11 vertices and bipartite instances on n≤12n\leq 12, we enumerate nonisomorphic nonempty graphs and first screen them using an O⁡(2n​m)O(2^{n}m) subset dynamic program for Greedy: since V⋆​(G)≥𝔼⁡[|Greedy⁡(G)|]V^{\star}(G)\geq\mathbb{E}[|\mathrm{Greedy{}}(G)|], only candidates whose Greedy ratio falls below the target threshold require exact evaluation of Equation (14). This screening greatly reduces the number of graphs requiring exact evaluation, e.g., among the 12 005 16712\,005\,167 nonisomorphic nonempty graphs on ten vertices, only 2121 have a Greedy ratio below 0.70.7.

Appendix A Missing Proofs in Section 4

In this section, we prove Lemmas 4.2, 4.3 and 4.5.

Proof of Lemma 4.2.

Fix the edge order σ\sigma and which edges between {x1,x2}\{x_{1},x_{2}\} and YY are retained. Recall that C=Be−x2C=B_{e}-x_{2}. Before the run on BeB_{e} first accepts an edge incident to x2x_{2}, both runs make identical decisions and agree on the matched status of every vertex in V⁡(C)V(C). If x2x_{2} remains unmatched at the end of the run on BeB_{e}, both runs agree on all of V⁡(C)V(C) and the equality holds trivially.

Suppose instead that x2x_{2} is matched in BeB_{e}, and let (x2,u)(x_{2},u) be the first edge incident to x2x_{2} accepted in BeB_{e}. Immediately after (x2,u)(x_{2},u) is accepted, uu is the unique vertex in V⁡(C)V(C) whose matched status differs between the two runs at this time (matched in BeB_{e}, free in CC). Next, we use induction on subsequent arrivals to prove that exactly one vertex in V⁡(C)V(C) has a different matched status between the two runs at any later time:

  • •

    Unless the arriving edge belongs to CC and is incident to uu, the unique differing vertex remains unchanged. Edges incident to x2x_{2} are rejected in BeB_{e} and absent from CC; all other such edges see identical endpoint statuses in both runs, so both runs make the same decision.

  • •

    Suppose an edge (u,w)∈E⁡(C)(u,w)\in E(C) arrives, where uu is the current unique differing vertex. Then w≠uw\neq u currently has the same status in both runs. If ww is already matched in both runs, both runs reject (u,w)(u,w). If ww is free in both runs, the run where uu is free accepts (u,w)(u,w), while the run where uu is already matched rejects (u,w)(u,w); after this step, uu is matched in both runs and ww becomes the unique differing vertex in V⁡(C)V(C).

At the end of the run, x2x_{2} is matched in BeB_{e}, contributing 33 to 3​N+2​R3N+2R, while at most one old vertex in V⁡(C)V(C) loses its matched status in BeB_{e} relative to CC. Such a loss has weight 33 if the vertex is x1x_{1}, weight 22 if it is a reference vertex, and weight 00 otherwise. The new contribution of x2x_{2} therefore compensates for this loss, proving 3​N+2​R≥3​N1+2​R1.3N+2R\geq 3N_{1}+2R_{1}. ∎

For t<τt<\tau, let p⁡(t)p(t) denote the probability that Greedy on BB has not matched ww by time tt, conditional on the fixed edges accepted by Greedy on HH and their arrival times.

Further reveal all arrivals in BB up to time tt. While ww remains unmatched in BB, it is unmatched in both runs. If zz is still unmatched in BB, the two runs agree on the matched status of every vertex in HH, and zz is the only additional unmatched vertex in BB. If zz is already matched in BB, the comparison in the proof of Lemma 4.2 ensures that at most one vertex is unmatched in BB but matched in HH. If (a,w)(a,w) exists and has not arrived, its remaining arrival time is uniform on (t,1)(t,1). Indeed, when a≠za\neq z, its fixed matching time in HH is already past; when a=za=z, its arrival time is unrestricted. Throughout this interval, the matched vertices in HH remain unchanged, while the unmatched vertices in BB can only disappear. Thus, the only edge that can match ww during this interval is the same edge (a,w)(a,w), when it exists. Its conditional probability of arriving during the interval is δ/(1−t)\delta/(1-t). Averaging over the arrivals revealed up to time tt, we obtain p⁡(t+δ)≥p⁡(t)⋅(1−δ1−t)p(t+\delta)\geq p(t)\cdot\left(1-\frac{\delta}{1-t}\right), which yields p⁡(t+δ)1−t−δ≥p⁡(t)1−t.\frac{p(t+\delta)}{1-t-\delta}\geq\frac{p(t)}{1-t}.

Hence, p⁡(t)/(1−t)p(t)/(1-t) is nondecreasing between consecutive fixed acceptance times of HH. If Greedy on D−(xi,yi)D-(x_{i},y_{i}) matches xix_{i}, adding (xi,yi)(x_{i},y_{i}) either leaves the run unchanged or matches xix_{i} earlier. Thus, 3​n+2​r≥3≥2+τ3n+2r\geq 3\geq 2+\tau.

Otherwise, this run agrees with Greedy on HH. If (xi,yi)(x_{i},y_{i}) is retained and arrives before τ\tau, it is accepted and contributes 55. If it arrives after τ\tau, then yiy_{i} is already matched and contributes 22. These disjoint events have probabilities q​τq\tau and 1−τ1-\tau, respectively. where the last inequality uses 5​q≥35q\geq 3. This calculation also covers τ=1\tau=1.

Proof of Lemma 4.5.

Let Ry2R_{y_{2}} and Ky2K_{y_{2}} indicate whether y2y_{2} is matched in M⁡(Be)M(B_{e}) and M⁡(B)M(B), respectively. We first prove

𝔼⁡[3​N+2​Ry2+2​Ky2]≥4.\mathbb{E}[3N+2R_{y_{2}}+2K_{y_{2}}]\geq 4.

Fix which edges between {x1,x2}\{x_{1},x_{2}\} and the non-reference vertices are retained. Consider a uniformly random arrival order of the edges of BB, these retained edges, and the two reference edges (x1,y2)(x_{1},y_{2}) and (x2,y2)(x_{2},y_{2}). Both reference edges are included in this order, while each is independently retained w.p. qq. Run Greedy on BB until either y2y_{2} is matched or an edge from {x1,x2}\{x_{1},x_{2}\} to a currently unmatched vertex of BB arrives.

Before this point, every arriving edge incident to x1x_{1} or x2x_{2} has its endpoint in BB already matched. Thus, x1,x2x_{1},x_{2} remain unmatched and the two runs agree on BB. If y2y_{2} is matched at this point, then 2​Ry2+2​Ky2=42R_{y_{2}}+2K_{y_{2}}=4.

Otherwise, assume the current edge is incident to x1x_{1}. Conditional on the arrived edges and their order, the remaining order is uniform. Neither reference edge arrived earlier, since either would have caused Greedy to stop. The current edge is therefore retained w.p. at least qq. In the following analysis, we discard the vertices of BB already matched in both runs, since they cannot be matched again.

If the current edge is retained, x1x_{1} contributes 33. If it also matches y2y_{2}, another 22 is obtained immediately. If it does not match y2y_{2}, apply Inequality (11) to x2,y2x_{2},y_{2} and the remaining graph after accepting this edge. Their conditional expected contribution is at least 3−1=23-1=2, since the probability that Greedy on this remaining graph matches y2y_{2} is at most 11. Thus, the conditional expected contribution is at least 55.

If the current edge is not retained, it must be (x1,y2)(x_{1},y_{2}). Apply Inequality (11) to x2,y2x_{2},y_{2}, then add x1x_{1} using Lemma 4.2, counting only y2y_{2} as a reference vertex. The conditional expectation of 3​N+2​Ry2+Ky23N+2R_{y_{2}}+K_{y_{2}} is at least 33, and the additional term Ky2K_{y_{2}} is nonnegative.

Thus, the conditional expected contribution is at least 5​q+3​(1−q)=3+2​q≥45q+3(1-q)=3+2q\geq 4. Averaging proves the claimed bound. Since R≥Ry2R\geq R_{y_{2}}, 𝔼⁡[Ky2]=μ2\mathbb{E}[K_{y_{2}}]=\mu_{2}, and 𝔼⁡[K]=μ1+μ2\mathbb{E}[K]=\mu_{1}+\mu_{2}, we conclude that

𝔼⁡[3​N+2​R+K]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[3N+2R+K] ≥𝔼⁡[3​N+2​Ry2+2​Ky2]+μ1−μ2≥4+μ1−μ2.∎\displaystyle\geq\mathbb{E}[3N+2R_{y_{2}}+2K_{y_{2}}]+\mu_{1}-\mu_{2}\geq 4+\mu_{1}-\mu_{2}.\qed

Appendix B A Stronger Guarantee for Triangle-Free Graphs

In this section, we prove Theorem 1.2 by fixing the parameters a=3/32,b=4/11,p=11/25a=3/32,b=4/11,p=11/25. When a shadow edge has two reference vertices, triangle-freeness rules out the cross edges to these vertices, allowing us to strengthen the local comparison from weights (3,2,1)(3,2,1) to (7,4,3)(7,4,3).

B.1 A Stronger Local Comparison

Fix HbH_{b} and a shadow edge e=(x1,x2)∈Tae=(x_{1},x_{2})\in T_{a}. Condition further on BB, as in Section 4.1. If ee arrives at time s<as<a, each edge between {x1,x2}\{x_{1},x_{2}\} and YY is independently retained with probability

q=1−b1−s≥1−b=711.q=\frac{1-b}{1-s}\geq 1-b=\frac{7}{11}.

We use the equivalent formulation with a common uniform edge order σ\sigma. Throughout this subsection, expectations are conditioned on HbH_{b} and BB, and we write k=kek=k_{e}.

Suppose that k=2k=2, with (x1,y1),(x2,y2)∈M∗(x_{1},y_{1}),(x_{2},y_{2})\in M^{*}. Since the original graph contains the shadow edge (x1,x2)(x_{1},x_{2}), the only edges between {x1,x2}\{x_{1},x_{2}\} and {y1,y2}\{y_{1},y_{2}\} before retention are (x1,y1)(x_{1},y_{1}) and (x2,y2)(x_{2},y_{2}). Otherwise, it would violate the triangle-freeness.

Recall that μi\mu_{i} denotes the probability that the reference vertex yiy_{i} is matched in M⁡(B)M(B) for each i∈{1,2}i\in\{1,2\}. Similar to Lemma 4.3, we show the following bound with different weights on nn and rr.

Lemma B.1.

Under the setup of Lemma 4.3, if q≥7/11q\geq 7/11, then

𝔼⁡[7​n+4​r]≥7−3​μi.\mathbb{E}[7n+4r]\geq 7-3\mu_{i}.

The bound also holds after fixing which edges incident to xix_{i}, other than (xi,yi)(x_{i},y_{i}), are retained.

Proof.

The proof of Lemma 4.3 applies with weights 77 and 44 in place of 33 and 22. The condition that 5​q≥35q\geq 3 used there is replaced by 11​q≥711q\geq 7, which holds by assumption. The same argument therefore proves the statement. ∎

Lemma B.2.

For the coupled matchings M⁡(B)M(B) and M⁡(Be)M(B_{e}), we have

𝔼⁡[7​N+4​R+3​K]≥7​k.\mathbb{E}[7N+4R+3K]\geq 7k.
Proof.

The case when k=0k=0 is immediate.

For k=1k=1, use the notation and the three cases from Section 4.2, with weights 7,4,37,4,3 on N1,R1,KN_{1},R_{1},K, respectively. In the first two cases, the contribution is at least 77. In the third case, its conditional expectation is 11​q≥711q\geq 7. Thus, we have 𝔼⁡[7​N1+4​R1+3​K]≥7\mathbb{E}[7N_{1}+4R_{1}+3K]\geq 7. The proof of Lemma 4.2 also applies with endpoint weight 77 and reference-vertex weight 44: the added endpoint contributes 77, while at most one old vertex loses its matched status, with weight at most 77. Hence, adding x2x_{2} gives 7​N+4​R≥7​N1+4​R17N+4R\geq 7N_{1}+4R_{1}, which proves the claim for k=1k=1.

Now suppose that k=2k=2. Recall the definition of LL from Section 4.3. Fix the retention choices for edges from {x1,x2}\{x_{1},x_{2}\} to Y∖{y1,y2}Y\setminus\{y_{1},y_{2}\}. For a triangle-free graph, the only counted edges between {x1,x2}\{x_{1},x_{2}\} and {y1,y2}\{y_{1},y_{2}\} are (x1,y1)(x_{1},y_{1}) and (x2,y2)(x_{2},y_{2}). As in Section 4.3, we prove the lemma when k=2k=2 by induction on LL. When L=2L=2, each reference edge contributes 1111 whenever retained, so

𝔼⁡[7​N+4​R+3​K]=22​q≥14.\mathbb{E}[7N+4R+3K]=22q\geq 14.

11+(7−3​μ2)+3​(μ1+μ2)=18+3​μ1.11+(7-3\mu_{2})+3(\mu_{1}+\mu_{2})=18+3\mu_{1}.

B.3 Verifying the Guarantee

Recall that we fix a=3/32a=3/32 and b=4/11b=4/11. For every integer n≥1n\geq 1, define

Lntf=1425+(1−a)n−(1−b)n2​n−350​(1−a)n−322​(1−b)n.L_{n}^{\mathrm{tf}}=\frac{14}{25}+\frac{(1-a)^{n}-(1-b)^{n}}{2n}-\frac{3}{50}(1-a)^{n}-\frac{3}{22}(1-b)^{n}.

Substituting Equation (8) into Inequality (15), we obtain

𝔼⁡[𝖠𝖫𝖦]𝖮𝖯𝖳≥∑n≥1cn⋅Lntf,cn≥0,∑n≥1cn=1.\frac{\mathbb{E}[\mathsf{ALG}]}{\mathsf{OPT}}\geq\sum_{n\geq 1}c_{n}\cdot L_{n}^{\mathrm{tf}},\qquad c_{n}\geq 0,\qquad\sum_{n\geq 1}c_{n}=1.
